name: Dhanusha Dham
tagline: Where a piece of Shiva's broken bow is said to rest
meta_description: Dhanusha Dham near Janakpur: the temple of Shiva's broken bow from the Ramayana, the Makar Sankranti mela, Maithil villages and how to visit from Janakpur.
summary: Dhanusha Dham is a Hindu pilgrimage town about 18 km from Janakpur, where devotees believe a fragment of Shiva's bow, broken by Rama to win Sita, lies in a temple. It draws crowds at Makar Sankranti in mid-January and gives a gentle look at Maithil village life. Visit as a half-day trip from Janakpur, October to March.
intro: In the Ramayana, Rama wins Sita's hand by lifting and breaking the great bow of Shiva at King Janaka's court. Pilgrims say the bow shattered into pieces that fell across Mithila, and that one piece lies here, about 18 km from Janakpur. The town takes its name from it: dhanush, bow, and dham, holy place. For pilgrims who have just seen Janakpur, it completes the story of Sita's wedding.

Dhanusha Dham is now a municipality, formed in 2014 by joining several villages, but it still feels rural. A concrete road runs from Janakpur through rice fields, mango groves and ponds. At the centre is the temple around the bow fragment, with smaller shrines, a pond and stalls selling flowers, sweets and sacred threads. Apart from the January fair, few outside visitors come, and the pace of life is slow.

Most visitors come on a half-day trip from Janakpur, by car in about 40 minutes or by bus in about 45. It pairs well with a morning in Janakpur's temples and an afternoon in Maithil villages, where you may see painted walls and women at work in the fields. Go in the morning, when the light is soft and the temple quiet, and return to Janakpur for lunch. From October to March the weather is comfortable; from April it is very hot.

story.title: The bow that won Sita
paras: Janakpur and Dhanusha Dham form a single story landscape for Hindu pilgrims. In Janakpur is the palace of Janaka and the wedding pavilion; at Dhanusha Dham is the bow. The episode of the bow, Shiva's dhanush, is one of the best known in the Ramayana and the reason the district itself is called Dhanusha. Rama's breaking of the bow is the moment that leads to his marriage, and the scene is still sung about in Maithil wedding songs.

For generations, pilgrims walking the circuits of Mithila have stopped here to worship at the fragment. The shrine has been rebuilt and enlarged over time, and a temple now stands around the remains. Priests tell visitors the story and point out what they say is the petrified piece of the bow. The atmosphere is devotional rather than grand; the shrine is modest, and the stories matter more than the architecture.

Every year at Makar Sankranti, in mid-January, Dhanusha Dham hosts a large fair. Pilgrims from Nepal and the Indian side of Mithila arrive to worship, bathe and eat the season's foods, and the fields around the temple fill with stalls and swings. The rest of the year it is a calm farming town. Children ride the swings, families buy tilkut and toys, and the smell of fried sweets hangs over the lanes.

legend: In the Ramayana, King Janaka set a test for Sita's suitors: string the great bow of Shiva. Kings and princes could not even move it. Rama lifted it with ease, and as he drew the string the bow broke with a sound like thunder. Local belief holds that one piece of that bow fell at this spot, where pilgrims now worship it in the Dhanusha temple.
people: Dhanusha Dham's people are Maithils, mostly farmers who grow rice, wheat, lentils and mangoes, with priests and shopkeepers serving the temple. Maithili is the home language, with Nepali and Hindi widely understood. Maithil women decorate their homes with painting for weddings and festivals, and some sell work through art groups in Janakpur.

untold.fact: Dhanushadham municipality was created on 18 May 2014 by merging the Govindapur, Umprempur, Yagyabhumi and Dhanushadham village development committees.
Dhanusha Dham lies about 18 km from Janakpur on a concrete road; local buses take about 45 minutes, and a festival is held here every year at Makar Sankranti.
The whole district, Dhanusha, takes its name from the bow (dhanush) of Shiva that Rama broke to win Sita, according to the Ramayana tradition honoured at this temple.

highlights.title: The Dhanusha temple
highlights.text: The temple built around what pilgrims revere as a fragment of Shiva's bow. Priests tell the story of Sita's swayamvar and show worshippers the sacred remains. Remove shoes and make an offering if you wish.

highlights.title: Makar Sankranti mela
highlights.text: In mid-January the town hosts a big fair. Pilgrims worship at the bow, buy tilkut and toys, and families picnic in the surrounding fields. Expect crowds and slow traffic from Janakpur.

highlights.title: Maithil village lanes
highlights.text: Around the temple, mud-walled houses, ponds and mango groves show rural Mithila. Before weddings and festivals some homes are freshly painted with Mithila designs. A local guide can introduce you to families.

highlights.title: A half day from Janakpur
highlights.text: The concrete road from Janakpur takes about 40 minutes by car through rice fields, making Dhanusha Dham an easy add-on to a Janakpur stay. Hire a car or e-rickshaw for the round trip.

highlights.title: Quiet temple mornings
highlights.text: Outside festival days, mornings are calm: a few families making offerings, priests reading, birds in the trees. It is a peaceful contrast to Janakpur's crowds. Mornings are the best time to visit.

how_to_reach.text: Dhanusha Dham is about 18 km from Janakpur on a concrete road, about 40 minutes by car or 45 minutes by local bus. Hire a car or e-rickshaw in Janakpur for a half-day round trip with waiting time.
Fly from Kathmandu to Janakpur (JKR) in about 25 to 30 minutes, then drive. Check current status before you travel, as winter fog can delay flights.

where_to_stay: There is no tourist accommodation of note at Dhanusha Dham itself. Stay in Janakpur, which has simple to mid-range city hotels about 40 minutes away, and visit Dhanusha Dham as a half-day trip. During the Makar Sankranti mela, Janakpur's hotels fill with pilgrims, so book ahead.
tips: Combine Dhanusha Dham with a morning at Janakpur's Janaki Mandir and ponds.
Remove shoes at the temple, dress modestly and ask before photographing the shrine.
Carry small notes for offerings and snacks; there are no ATMs at the temple.
Expect heavy crowds and slow traffic on Makar Sankranti; go early.
Bring water and a hat; there is little shade on the road and around the temple.

experiences.title: Visit the temple of Shiva's bow
experiences.summary: See the temple where pilgrims worship what they believe is a fragment of Shiva's bow, broken by Rama to win Sita, and hear the story from the priests who tend it. Allow about an hour.
body: The Dhanusha temple stands at the centre of the town, surrounded by smaller shrines, trees and a pond. Pilgrims enter with flowers, sweets and incense, and the priests guide them to the sacred remains that local tradition identifies as part of Shiva's bow. Small stalls by the gate sell flowers, incense and sweets for offerings.

Ask your guide or a priest to tell the story of the swayamvar, the ceremony in which Sita chose her husband. Many versions are told in Maithili songs, and older visitors often join in. The temple has been rebuilt over the years, and you can see newer construction around the older shrine. Pilgrims from the Indian side of Mithila often visit as part of a wider circuit of Ramayana sites.

Remove shoes before entering, dress modestly and make a small offering if you wish. Photography of the inner shrine may not be allowed; ask first. Mornings are quiet and cool, the best time to visit. Combine the visit with a walk through the village or tea at a stall by the gate, and keep small notes for donations.

faqs.q: What is at Dhanusha Dham?
faqs.a: Dhanusha Dham has a temple built around what Hindu pilgrims believe is a fragment of Shiva's bow, broken by Rama during Sita's swayamvar in the Ramayana. There are also smaller shrines, a pond, stalls and the surrounding Maithil village. A mela is held at Makar Sankranti.

faqs.q: How far is Dhanusha Dham from Janakpur?
faqs.a: About 18 km on a concrete road, roughly 40 minutes by car or 45 minutes by local bus. Most visitors make it a half-day trip from Janakpur, combining it with the Janaki Mandir and other sites in the city. Hiring a car gives you more flexibility.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at Dhanusha Dham?
faqs.a: There is usually no fixed entry fee for the temple. Visitors may make a donation or offering, and priests may ask for a small amount for a blessing or puja. Carry small notes and decide what you are comfortable giving.

experiences.title: Makar Sankranti fair at Dhanusha Dham
experiences.summary: Join the mid-January mela, when pilgrims from Nepal and the Indian side of Mithila crowd the temple of the bow, bathe, buy tilkut and toys at the stalls, and families picnic in the fields. Go early in the morning.
body: Makar Sankranti, which Nepal's hill communities call Maghe Sankranti and Maithils often call Sakrait, marks the sun's move into Capricorn in mid-January. In Mithila it is a day for bathing, worship and eating dahi-chura, beaten rice with yogurt, and tilkut, a sesame sweet. The festival follows the solar calendar, so it falls on almost the same date each year, unlike most Hindu festivals, which follow the moon.

At Dhanusha Dham the day brings a large fair. From early morning pilgrims queue at the temple, priests are busy with blessings, and the lanes fill with stalls selling tilkut, chura, sugar toys, bangles and religious pictures. Swings and small rides appear for children. Many families come for the day from nearby villages, bringing food and blankets to sit on.

Go early to see the worship before the crowds peak, keep valuables safe and agree on a meeting point with your group. Traffic from Janakpur is heavy; leave plenty of time. Check current status before you travel for the exact date each year. Photographs of the fair are usually welcome, but ask before taking close portraits.

faqs.q: When is the Makar Sankranti fair at Dhanusha Dham?
faqs.a: It is held on Makar Sankranti, the first day of the month of Magh, usually 14 or 15 January. The main worship is in the morning, and the fair continues through the day. Check current status before you travel for the exact date each year.

faqs.q: What do people eat at Makar Sankranti in Mithila?
faqs.a: Maithil families eat dahi-chura, beaten rice with thick yogurt and jaggery, along with tilkut, a pounded sesame and jaggery sweet, and other sesame sweets. Khichdi is often eaten in the evening. Stalls at Dhanusha Dham sell tilkut and chura in large quantities.

faqs.q: Is the Dhanusha Dham fair crowded?
faqs.a: Yes, especially in the morning, when pilgrims from Nepal and the Indian side of Mithila arrive. Expect queues at the temple, packed lanes and slow traffic from Janakpur. It is a cheerful crowd, but keep valuables safe and stay with your guide.

experiences.title: Walk the Maithil villages and painted walls
experiences.image_query: Mithila painted house wall village Nepal
experiences.summary: Walk village lanes around Dhanusha Dham with a local guide, past mud-walled houses, ponds and mango groves, and look for Mithila wall paintings made by women for weddings and festivals. Go with a local guide.
body: Rural Mithila is a landscape of ponds, mango and bamboo groves and rice fields, with villages of mud and brick houses built close together. A walk with a local guide around Dhanusha Dham shows how families live: courtyards where grain dries, buffalo tethered in the shade, women grinding spices. Many houses have a small shrine in the courtyard, often marked with vermilion.

Maithil women paint the walls of their houses for weddings, births and festivals. Kohbar paintings of lotus, bamboo, fish and parrots decorate the wedding chamber; aripan patterns in rice paste mark floors before rituals. Depending on the season, you may see fresh paintings or faded ones from the last wedding. Some paintings are bold and new, others faded by sun and rain.

Ask your guide to introduce you rather than walking into courtyards. Photographs of paintings are usually welcomed if you ask; photographs of women should only be taken with clear consent. A small purchase or tip to a painter is a good way to say thanks. Walks are flat and short, usually about two hours, and best in the morning or late afternoon.

faqs.q: Can I see Mithila wall paintings in villages?
faqs.a: Yes, often, though it depends on the season. Paintings are made for weddings, festivals and rituals, so they are freshest around the wedding season and festivals such as Chhath and Tihar. A local guide can take you to homes where painting is still practised.

faqs.q: What are kohbar and aripan?
faqs.a: Kohbar is the painting on the walls of a Maithil wedding chamber, full of symbols of fertility and long marriage such as lotus, bamboo and fish. Aripan is floor painting in rice paste, drawn by women before rituals and festivals. Both are central to Mithila art.

faqs.q: Is it respectful to visit village homes?
faqs.a: Yes, when done with a local guide and permission. Ask before entering courtyards and taking photographs, dress modestly and remove shoes where asked. Keep visits short and friendly. Families are often proud to show their paintings.

experiences.title: A Maithil dahi-chura breakfast
experiences.best_time: Morning, all year; essential in January
experiences.summary: Eat the simplest and most loved Maithil breakfast: chura, beaten rice, with thick dahi, jaggery or sugar and, in January, tilkut. Ask your guide for a village sweet shop or a family table. It is cheap and filling.
body: Dahi-chura is everyday food in Mithila and a festival food at Makar Sankranti. Chura is rice that has been parboiled, flattened and dried, so it keeps for months. Mixed with thick, slightly sour dahi and sweetened with jaggery or sugar, it makes a cool, filling breakfast. Families often buy chura in bulk after the rice harvest.

In January it comes with tilkut, made by pounding roasted sesame with jaggery into crumbly discs, and sometimes with vegetable curry or pickle on the side. Many families also eat khichdi, rice and lentils cooked together, on the evening of the festival. In many Maithil homes it is served on Makar Sankranti morning, after the family bath.

Sweet shops and small eateries around Dhanusha Dham and Janakpur serve dahi-chura in the mornings. Look for fresh dahi set in clay pots. It is vegetarian, gentle on the stomach and a good start to a day of temple visits. Portions are generous; a small bowl is enough before a morning of sightseeing.

faqs.q: What is dahi-chura?
faqs.a: Dahi-chura is a Maithil dish of chura, beaten rice, mixed with dahi, thick yogurt, and sweetened with jaggery or sugar. It is a common breakfast in Mithila and the special food of Makar Sankranti in mid-January, often eaten with tilkut, a sesame sweet.

faqs.q: What is tilkut?
faqs.a: Tilkut is a sweet made by pounding roasted sesame seeds with jaggery or sugar into flat, crumbly cakes. It is a speciality of the Mithila and Magadh regions and is eaten especially around Makar Sankranti. Stalls at Dhanusha Dham and shops in Janakpur sell it in January.

faqs.q: Is dahi-chura safe for travellers to eat?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if the dahi is fresh and from a busy shop with good turnover. Look for yogurt set in clean clay pots. Travellers with sensitive stomachs might start with a small portion. It is vegetarian and contains dairy. Avoid it if the dahi smells off.

faqs.q: What is Dhanusha Dham famous for?
faqs.a: Dhanusha Dham is famous for its temple built around what Hindu pilgrims believe is a fragment of Shiva's bow, broken by Rama to win Sita in the Ramayana. The town and the whole district of Dhanusha are named after this bow. A large fair is held at Makar Sankranti each January.

faqs.q: How do I get to Dhanusha Dham from Janakpur?
faqs.a: Drive about 18 km on a concrete road, roughly 40 minutes by car, or take a local bus, about 45 minutes. Hiring a car or e-rickshaw in Janakpur for a half-day round trip is easiest and lets you stop in villages on the way.

faqs.q: How long should I spend at Dhanusha Dham?
faqs.a: A half day is enough for most visitors, including travel from Janakpur, the temple visit and a short village walk. On Makar Sankranti allow more time because of crowds and traffic. Most visitors return to Janakpur for lunch.

faqs.q: Is Dhanusha Dham worth visiting?
faqs.a: For travellers interested in the Ramayana, Hindu pilgrimage or rural Mithila, yes. The temple itself is modest, but the story, the village setting and the festival make it a rewarding half day from Janakpur. Travellers short on time may prefer to focus on Janakpur.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Dhanusha Dham?
faqs.a: October to March, when the weather is pleasant. Mid-January brings the Makar Sankranti fair, the busiest and most colourful day. From April to June temperatures often pass 40 °C, and the monsoon from late June to September brings heavy rain.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Dhanusha Dham?
faqs.a: There are no tourist hotels of note in Dhanusha Dham. Most visitors stay in Janakpur, about 40 minutes away, which has simple to mid-range hotels. Plan Dhanusha Dham as a half-day trip from Janakpur. Book ahead for festival dates.

faqs.q: Is the bow at Dhanusha Dham real?
faqs.a: Pilgrims revere what they believe is a petrified fragment of Shiva's bow from the Ramayana. It is a matter of faith rather than history. Visitors of all beliefs are welcome to see the shrine respectfully and hear the story from the priests.

faqs.q: What should I wear at Dhanusha Dham?
faqs.a: Light, loose clothes that cover shoulders and knees. Shoes come off at the temple, so sandals are practical. Bring a hat and sunscreen for the open roads, and a warm layer for January mornings, which can be foggy and cold.

faqs.q: Can I combine Dhanusha Dham with Koshi Tappu?
faqs.a: Yes, on a longer trip east. From Janakpur and Dhanusha Dham, drive east along the East-West Highway to Koshi Tappu, about 4 to 5 hours. Many travellers break the trip with a night in Janakpur and then continue to the Koshi floodplain for birds and wild buffalo.
